Prevention: Plant early in the season, or use early-maturing varieties, so that harvest can be completed before the dry season when the soil dries and crack (weevils reside in cracks).
Cuttings: vine-tips should be clean, especially the tender tips (the top 25-50 cm).
Treat using a pre-plant dip to provide control for the first few months:
Dip the cuttings into a solution of the fungus
Beauveria bassiana for 10-15 minutes prior to planting.
Avoid using tubers for planting as they may contain weevil larvae.
Use deep rooting varieties with long necks - adult weevils cannot burrow below 1 cm.
Maintain deep root depth; use a hoe to create a small hill or mound of soil around the base of the plant and re-ridge about 30 days after planting.
Or use a ground cover such as straw or plastic.
Irrigate regularly to prevent the soil from drying and cracking.
Encourage generalist predators of the weevil e.g. ants, spiders, carabids, and earwigs by planting hedgerows.
Remove alternative host plants (e.g. morning glory, wild spinach, wild
Ipomoea) and volunteer plants from in and around the field.
Plant new sweet potato crop at least 1 km away from infested fields (weevils cannot easily fly from field to field).
Harvest as soon as crop is mature and avoid piecemeal harvesting.
Rotate with a non-host crop, such as sorghum, rice or legumes, for 2 or 3 seasons.
Monitoring: Monitoring
Additional relevant crops: coffee, morning glory, sesame, cowpea, maize.
Monitor for weevils early in the crop season:
Eggs:
Yellowish-white, shiny and oval-shaped.
Pupae: 5-6 mm long and initially creamy white but become grey as they get older.
Larvae: chunky white legless grubs, about 5-10 mm long and slightly curved; the head is brown or light yellow.
Adults: black and shiny blue with long slender bodies (6-8 mm long), and a long snout with antennas on both sides.
Adults are mostly active at night and hide under leaves or in soil cracks during the day.
Look out for signs of the weevil:
Young plants (before storage roots form): small tunnels in lower base of stem where larvae feed.
Also, adults can be found on the leaves and vines, leaving small round feeding holes.
Storage root: tunnels which become brown, soft and spongy.
The damaged tissue has a bad smell.
Stems: turn yellow, crack, and wilt.
This can cause seedlings to die.
Look for feeding holes and larvae tunnels at the base (lower 10 cm) of the stems.

If damage to the stems is detected, dig up the roots of a few plants and inspect the surface of the roots for deep feeding punctures and cavities plugged with frass, and inspect the tunnels for larvae.
Place pheromone traps in the field at a radius of 280 m to catch the weevils.
Dry and hot temperatures between 27-30°C favour the development of weevils.
Direct Control: During crop growth, remove all infested sweet potato vines and storage roots and destroy by feeding to livestock or burning.
Do not bury remains as weevils can still survive and do not store remains near fields.
After harvest, flood the field for 24 hours after harvest to drown and kill the weevils.
Destroy all remains of the old crop and volunteer plants, particularly infested vines and tubers.
Do not store roots that show symptoms with non-infested roots.
Weevils can continue to cause damage during post-harvest storage.
